headings.title: Introduction to Acquired Immune Deficiencies
headings.content: Acquired immune deficiencies represent a significant disruption in the body's natural defense mechanisms, occurring after birth and throughout an individual's lifetime, unlike primary immunodeficiencies which are typically genetic. For nursing students preparing for clinical practice and professional board examinations in Nigeria, understanding acquired immune deficiencies is vital due to the high burden of infectious diseases and socio-economic factors influencing public health. An acquired immune deficiency develops when an external factor or secondary condition damages an immune system that was previously functioning normally. These factors can range from viral infections, such as the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), to severe malnutrition, malignancies, immunosuppressive medications, and metabolic disorders. When the immune system is compromised, the body loses its ability to protect itself effectively against opportunistic pathogens, neoplasms, and foreign invaders. Consequently, patients present with recurrent, severe, and unusual infections that standard treatments struggle to resolve. Recognizing the distinction between primary and acquired immune deficiencies helps nurses tailor holistic care plans, focusing heavily on prevention, early detection, and supportive management. Furthermore, comprehensive nursing care involves addressing the psychosocial stigma often associated with acquired immune deficiencies, ensuring that patients receive compassionate, non-judgmental support throughout their healthcare journey in diverse Nigerian clinical settings.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Mechanisms of Immune System Decline
headings.content: The pathophysiology of acquired immune deficiencies involves a progressive breakdown of the complex cellular and humoral components that maintain immunological homeostasis. At the core of this decline is often the depletion, functional impairment, or suppression of key immune cells, particularly CD4+ T-helper lymphocytes, which play a central coordinating role in both cellular and humoral immunity. When these regulatory cells are destroyed or exhausted, the communication network of the immune system collapses, impairing the activation of cytotoxic T cells and B cells. Consequently, antibody production decreases, and cell-mediated immunity fails. Pathogens that are normally cleared easily by a healthy immune system can now replicate unchecked. In addition to cellular destruction, chronic immune activation and persistent systemic inflammation can exhaust the remaining immune cells, leading to a state of immune senescence or exhaustion. As the immune system continuously attempts to fight off persistent antigens without adequate regulatory control, lymphoid tissues become damaged, further reducing the body's capacity to generate new, naive immune cells. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for nursing students, as it explains why patients with acquired immune deficiencies suffer from multiple opportunistic infections, experience delayed wound healing, and are at a heightened risk for various malignancies.

headings.title: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) and Progression to AIDS
headings.content: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) remains one of the most prominent and thoroughly studied causes of acquired immune deficiency globally and within Nigeria. HIV is a retrovirus that selectively targets, infects, and destroys cells bearing CD4 receptors, primarily CD4+ T-lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells. The viral life cycle involves binding to the host cell, fusion, reverse transcription of viral RNA into DNA, integration into the host genome, replication, and budding of new viral particles. Over time, this relentless viral replication leads to a steady decline in the absolute CD4+ T-cell count, gradually weakening the host's immune system. Without therapeutic intervention, the infection progresses through distinct clinical stages, eventually culminating in Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS). AIDS is clinically defined by a CD4+ T-cell count dropping below 200 cells/mm3 or the development of specific AIDS-defining illnesses, such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, Kaposi's sarcoma, cryptococcal meningitis, or severe wasting syndrome. Nurses must understand this progression to monitor patient status effectively, administer antiretroviral therapy (ART) education, and identify early warning signs of opportunistic infections during routine clinical assessments.

headings.title: Secondary Immunodeficiencies Caused by Malnutrition and Infections
headings.content: Beyond viral pathogens like HIV, secondary immunodeficiencies are frequently precipitated by environmental, nutritional, and infectious factors that compromise immune function. Severe acute malnutrition, prevalent in certain vulnerable populations, significantly impairs immune competence by depriving the body of essential macro- and micronutrients required for leukocyte production, antibody synthesis, and cellular repair. Conditions such as protein-energy malnutrition (kwashiorkor and marasmus) lead to thymic atrophy, reduced complement system proteins, and depressed phagocytic activity, rendering the individual highly susceptible to overwhelming infections. Additionally, chronic systemic infections such as tuberculosis, malaria, and measles can temporarily or persistently depress the immune system. Malaria, for instance, can impair splenic function and macrophage activity, while measles induces profound immune amnesia, wiping out previously acquired immunological memory cells and leaving the host vulnerable to secondary bacterial and viral infections. For nurses practicing in resource-constrained environments, recognizing the synergistic relationship between malnutrition and infection is critical. Comprehensive patient assessment must therefore incorporate nutritional screening alongside infection surveillance, ensuring that dietary rehabilitation and aggressive infection control are prioritized in the nursing care plan.

headings.title: Iatrogenic Causes of Acquired Immune Deficiency
headings.content: Iatrogenic causes of acquired immune deficiency are those induced directly by medical interventions, treatments, or procedures. In modern healthcare, immunosuppressive therapy is frequently employed to manage autoimmune disorders, prevent solid organ or bone marrow transplant rejection, and treat various malignancies. Medications such as corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents, and biologic therapies intentionally dampen the immune response to achieve therapeutic goals, but they simultaneously leave patients in a state of secondary immunodeficiency. For instance, high-dose corticosteroids inhibit inflammatory cytokine production and induce lymphocyte apoptosis, while chemotherapy agents indiscriminately destroy rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow precursors responsible for white blood cell production. Consequently, iatrogenically immunosuppressed patients face severe risks of opportunistic infections, ranging from cytomegalovirus and fungal infections to atypical bacterial pneumonia. Nursing students must recognize that patients undergoing chemotherapy, radiation, or chronic immunosuppressive therapy require rigorous protective isolation protocols, meticulous hand hygiene, strict monitoring for subtle signs of infection like low-grade fevers, and prompt reporting of any pathological deviations to the medical team.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Clinical assessment and diagnostic evaluation of acquired immune deficiencies require a systematic, thorough approach by the nurse and healthcare team. The nursing assessment begins with a detailed health history focusing on recurrent infections, unexplained weight loss, chronic fatigue, night sweats, travel history, nutritional status, and any history of immunosuppressive drug use or high-risk behaviors. Physical examination entails carefully inspecting the skin, oral cavity for candidiasis, lymph nodes for generalized lymphadenopathy, and the respiratory system for signs of opportunistic pneumonia. Diagnostically, laboratory investigations are paramount. Complete Blood Count (CBC) with differential frequently reveals leukopenia, lymphopenia, or anemia. Specific diagnostic assays include HIV antibody and antigen screening tests (rapid diagnostic tests and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays), confirmatory Western blot or molecular nucleic acid testing (NAT), and CD4+ T-lymphocyte subset enumeration to stage the severity of immune decline. Furthermore, viral load quantification helps monitor disease progression and the efficacy of therapeutic regimens. Nurses play a pivotal role in preparing patients for these diagnostic tests, providing pre- and post-test counseling, ensuring specimen integrity, and helping patients interpret the clinical significance of their results with empathy and professional discretion.

headings.title: Nursing Management and Patient Care Strategies
headings.content: Nursing management and patient care strategies for individuals with acquired immune deficiencies focus on infection prevention, promotion of optimal nutrition, medication adherence support, and psychological rehabilitation. Because these patients are highly vulnerable to opportunistic pathogens, nurses must implement strict infection control measures, including standard precautions, meticulous hand hygiene, and patient education on avoiding crowds, raw foods, and environmental hazards. Nutritional support is equally critical; nurses should collaborate with dietitians to provide high-protein, high-calorie meals that support immune function and prevent severe wasting. For patients prescribed Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) or prophylactic medications, nursing interventions must center on adherence counseling. Non-adherence leads to treatment failure, viral resistance, and accelerated disease progression. Nurses can utilize pillboxes, treatment buddies, and digital reminders to help patients manage complex drug regimens. Psychologically, patients often face profound stigma, anxiety, and depression. Providing empathetic listening, establishing a trusting nurse-patient relationship, and connecting patients with peer support groups or professional mental health counselors are vital components of comprehensive, holistic nursing care.

headings.title: Prevention, Treatment, and Public Health Considerations in Nigeria
headings.content: Addressing acquired immune deficiencies from a public health perspective requires a multi-faceted approach encompassing prevention, accessible treatment, and community education, especially within the context of Nigeria. Public health strategies heavily emphasize prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), routine voluntary counseling and testing (VCT), widespread distribution of antiretroviral medications, and aggressive public awareness campaigns to reduce societal stigma. In Nigeria, healthcare infrastructure challenges, cultural beliefs, and economic barriers can hinder effective disease management. Therefore, nurses act as frontline public health advocates, delivering health education in community clinics, primary health care centers, and rural outreach programs. They promote safe practices, distribute barrier methods like condoms, and facilitate linkage-to-care systems to ensure diagnosed individuals immediately commence and maintain lifelong ART. Furthermore, integrating nutritional supplementation programs into HIV and infectious disease clinics helps combat the dual burden of malnutrition and secondary immunodeficiencies. By championing policy changes, advocating for adequate healthcare resources, and fostering community-based support networks, nurses significantly contribute to lowering the national prevalence of acquired immune deficiencies and improving overall health outcomes across Nigerian communities.
